A qq-microscope for mock-theta denominator patterns

Mohamed El Bachraoui Address: Dept. Math. Sci, United Arab Emirates University, PO Box 15551, Al-Ain, UAE Email address: melbachraoui@uaeu.ac.ae
Date: September 5, 2026
Abstract.

We give a systematic creative-microscoping treatment of truncated basic hypergeometric sums attached to three classical third-order mock theta denominator patterns, represented by ϕ⁡(q)\phi(q), ω⁡(q)\omega(q), and ν⁡(q)\nu(q). The main conceptual point is that these denominator patterns naturally admit exact finite theta evaluations at a=q±na=q^{\pm n}, microscopic qq-supercongruences, and cyclotomic/pp-adic consequences within a single framework. For

S⁡(q,a):=∑n≥0q2​n+1​(a​q,q/a,q2)n(−q2,q2)n,S(q,a):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{2n+1}(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{n}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}},

we prove, for odd nn, a finite theta evaluation at a=q±na=q^{\pm n}, equivalently a microscopic qq-supercongruence. We prove an analogous finite theta evaluation for the ν\nu-type denominator

Nm​(q,a):=∑j=0mq2​j+1​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(−q,q2)j+1.N_{m}(q,a):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j+1}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(-q;q^{2})_{j+1}}.

We then introduce the one-parameter denominator family

𝒯⁡(q,b):=∑n≥0q2​n​(q,q2)n2(q2,q2)n​(b,q2)n,\mathcal{T}(q;b):=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{2n}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{n}^{2}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{n}(b;q^{2})_{n}},

whose specializations include the ω\omega-type shifted denominator (b=q3b=q^{3}) and the two-color family (b=q2​kb=q^{2k}). For its truncated aa-extension we obtain an exact evaluation at a=q±na=q^{\pm n}, deduce microscopic congruences modulo (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}), and derive cyclotomic consequences, including zero congruences in the q2​kq^{2k}-subfamily and nontrivial pp-adic versions for the cases b=qb=q and b=q3b=q^{3}.

Key words and phrases: 
qq-series, basic hypergeometric series, mock theta functions, creative microscoping, qq-supercongruences
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
33D15, 11A07, 11B65

1. Introduction

The purpose of this paper is to show that several classical mock-theta denominator patterns admit a common creative-microscoping treatment. For truncated basic hypergeometric sums attached to the ϕ\phi-, ω\omega-, and ν\nu-type denominators, we obtain exact evaluations at the odd specializations a=q±na=q^{\pm n} and deduce microscopic qq-supercongruences together with cyclotomic and pp-adic consequences. Thus the point of view is that the arithmetic structure is carried by the denominator patterns themselves, rather than by isolated congruence examples.

The present paper is organized around three classical third-order mock theta denominator patterns:

(−q2,q2)n,(q,q2)n+1,(−q,q2)n+1.(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n},\qquad(q;q^{2})_{n+1},\qquad(-q;q^{2})_{n+1}.

These are represented, respectively, by Ramanujan’s function

ϕ⁡(q):=∑n≥0qn2(−q2,q2)n,\phi(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{n^{2}}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}}, (1.1)

the alternative series

ω⁡(q):=∑n≥0qn(q,q2)n+1,\omega(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{n}}{(q;q^{2})_{n+1}}, (1.2)

and Watson’s function

ν⁡(q):=∑n≥0qn⁡(n+1)(−q,q2)n+1.\nu(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(-q;q^{2})_{n+1}}. (1.3)

The same three functions also appear naturally in the partition-theoretic work of Andrews, Dixit and Yee [2].

Our starting point is the qq-hypergeometric series

S⁡(q):=∑n≥0q2​n+1​(q,q2)n2(−q2,q2)n,S(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{2n+1}(q;q^{2})_{n}^{2}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}}, (1.4)

which recently arose in [4, 5] in connection with two-color partitions. Although (1.4) was originally motivated there by ω⁡(q)\omega(q), its denominator places it more naturally in the ϕ\phi-type category (1.1). In this paper the main results are grouped by denominator pattern and the two-color material is treated later as a specialization. This organization is meant to emphasize that the two-color congruences arise from a broader mock-theta denominator framework rather than as isolated examples.

For completeness, we note that the first two denominator patterns also occur in McIntosh’s second-order mock theta functions. In particular,

μ⁡(q)=∑n≥0(−1)n​qn2​(q,q2)n(−q2,q2)n2\mu(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{n}q^{n^{2}}(q;q^{2})_{n}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}^{2}} (1.5)

again involves the factor (−q2,q2)n(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}; see [20]. We mention this only as background, since the exposition below is organized around the third-order trio (1.1)–(1.3).

Throughout, (a,q)n:=∏j=0n−1(1−a​qj)(a;q)_{n}:=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1-aq^{j}) denotes the qq-Pochhammer symbol and (a1,…,ar,q)n:=∏i=1r(ai,q)n(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r};q)_{n}:=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(a_{i};q)_{n}. For nonnegative integer mm and nn we use [nm]q{n\brack m}_{q} for the qq-binomial coefficient given by

[nm]=[nm]q={(q,q)n(q,q)m​(q,q)n−m​if ​n≥m,0​otherwise.{n\brack m}={n\brack m}_{q}=\begin{cases}\frac{(q;q)_{n}}{(q;q)_{m}(q;q)_{n-m}}\ \text{if\ }n\geq m,\\ 0\ \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Let ℤ⁡[q]\mathbb{Z}[q] denote the set of polynomials in qq with integer coefficients and let ℤ⁡(q)\mathbb{Z}(q) denote the set of rational functions in qq with integer coefficients. The nn-th cyclotomic polynomial is the polynomial in ℤ⁡[q]\mathbb{Z}[q] given by

Φn​(q)=∏j=1gcd⁡(j,n)=1n(q−ζj),\Phi_{n}(q)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\ \gcd(j,n)=1\end{subarray}}^{n}(q-\zeta^{j}),

where ζ=e2​π​i/n\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n} is the nn-th root of unity. Given polynomials A1​(q),A2​(q),P⁡(q)∈ℤ⁡[q]A_{1}(q),A_{2}(q),P(q)\in\mathbb{Z}[q], the congruence A1​(q)A2​(q)≡0(modP⁡(q))\frac{A_{1}(q)}{A_{2}(q)}\equiv 0\pmod{P(q)} means that P⁡(q)P(q) divides A1​(q)A_{1}(q) and that gcd⁡(P⁡(q),A2​(q))=1\gcd\big(P(q),A_{2}(q)\big)=1; and in general for rational functions A⁡(q),B⁡(q)∈ℤ⁡(q)A(q),B(q)\in\mathbb{Z}(q), the congruence A⁡(q)≡B⁡(q)(modP⁡(q))A(q)\equiv B(q)\pmod{P(q)} means that A⁡(q)−B⁡(q)≡0(modP⁡(q))A(q)-B(q)\equiv 0\pmod{P(q)}.

A guiding method in the subject is creative microscoping, introduced by Guo and Zudilin [14], which turns congruences modulo powers of cyclotomic polynomials into parameterized identities at roots of unity. Recent developments in this direction include Jackson’s transformations, Gasper’s Karlsson–Minton type summations, squares and higher-fold basic hypergeometric series, and higher-power cyclotomic congruences; see, for example, [16, 17, 18, 22].

From a historical point of view, this emphasis on roots of unity is not accidental. In modern language, Ramanujan’s original definition is already qq-microscopic in spirit: it is a root-by-root comparison between a mock theta function and a local theta correction. Indeed, in his last letter to Hardy, Ramanujan requires that for each root of unity ξ\xi there exist a modular form Mξ​(q)M_{\xi}(q) and a rational number α\alpha such that F⁡(q)−qα​Mξ​(q)F(q)-q^{\alpha}M_{\xi}(q) remains bounded as q→ξq\to\xi radially, while no single modular form works uniformly at all roots of unity; see [6, pp. 220–223] and the modern formulations in [19, 7]. Conversely, creative microscoping is built precisely on evaluating truncated basic hypergeometric series at roots of unity, and Guo and Zudilin explicitly observed that this perspective is close in spirit to the study of mock theta functions and quantum modular forms [14, p. 4]. It is therefore striking that these two literatures have so rarely met directly. To the best of our knowledge, the classical mock theta series themselves have not previously been treated in the language of creative microscoping or cyclotomic qq-supercongruences in any systematic way. Existing arithmetic work on mock theta functions has concentrated mainly on coefficient congruences and related partition congruences [1, 3, 21], while the root-of-unity side has largely been pursued through radial limits and quantum or antiquantum qq-series identities [7, 9, 10, 11]. This historical parallel motivates the viewpoint adopted here: the classical mock-theta denominator patterns themselves naturally support microscopic congruences and exact finite theta evaluations. More specifically, the ϕ\phi- and ν\nu-type cases lead to explicit finite theta formulas at a=q±na=q^{\pm n}, while the one-parameter family 𝒯⁡(q,b)\mathcal{T}(q;b) simultaneously captures the shifted ω\omega-type case and the two-color q2​kq^{2k}-family, leading in turn to cyclotomic and pp-adic consequences. In this sense, the paper is intended as a systematic creative-microscoping treatment of classical mock-theta denominator patterns rather than merely a collection of separate congruences.

Define the two-parameter series

S⁡(q,a):=∑n≥0q2​n+1​(a​q,q/a,q2)n(−q2,q2)nS(q,a):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{q^{2n+1}(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{n}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}} (1.6)

and, for odd n=2​m+1n=2m+1,

Sm​(q,a):=∑j=0mq2​j+1​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(−q2,q2)j.S_{m}(q,a):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\frac{q^{2j+1}(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{j}}.

Our first result is a finite theta evaluation for the ϕ\phi-type denominator.

Theorem 1.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Then

∑j=0mq2​j+1​(q1−n,qn+1,q2)j(−q2,q2)j=(−1)m​q2​m​(m+1)+1​∑r=−mm(−1)r​q−2​r2.\sum_{j=0}^{m}\frac{q^{2j+1}(q^{1-n},q^{n+1};q^{2})_{j}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{j}}=(-1)^{m}q^{2m(m+1)+1}\sum_{r=-m}^{m}(-1)^{r}q^{-2r^{2}}. (1.7)
Corollary 1.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Then modulo (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}), we have

∑j=0mq2​j+1​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(−q2,q2)j\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m}\frac{q^{2j+1}(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{j}} ≡(−1)m​q2​m​(m+1)+1​∑r=−mm(−1)r​q−2​r2.\displaystyle\equiv(-1)^{m}q^{2m(m+1)+1}\sum_{r=-m}^{m}(-1)^{r}q^{-2r^{2}}. (1.8)

The ν\nu-type analogue is obtained by replacing (−q2,q2)j(-q^{2};q^{2})_{j} with (−q,q2)j+1(-q;q^{2})_{j+1}.

Theorem 2.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd, and define

Nm​(q,a):=∑j=0mq2​j+1​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(−q,q2)j+1.N_{m}(q,a):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j+1}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(-q;q^{2})_{j+1}}.

Then

(1+qn)​∑j=0mq2​j+1​(q1−n,qn+1,q2)j(−q,q2)j+1=(−1)m​q(m+1)​(2​m+1)​∑r=−mm(−1)r​q−2​r2−r.(1+q^{n})\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j+1}\frac{(q^{1-n},q^{n+1};q^{2})_{j}}{(-q;q^{2})_{j+1}}=(-1)^{m}q^{(m+1)(2m+1)}\sum_{r=-m}^{m}(-1)^{r}q^{-2r^{2}-r}. (1.9)
Corollary 2.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Then modulo (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}), we have

(1+qn)​Nm​(q,a)≡(−1)m​q(m+1)​(2​m+1)​∑r=−mm(−1)r​q−2​r2−r.(1+q^{n})N_{m}(q,a)\equiv(-1)^{m}q^{(m+1)(2m+1)}\sum_{r=-m}^{m}(-1)^{r}q^{-2r^{2}-r}. (1.10)

The second main object in the paper is the one-parameter denominator family

𝒯⁡(q,b):=∑n≥0q2​n​(q,q2)n2(q2,q2)n​(b,q2)n.\mathcal{T}(q;b):=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{2n}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{n}^{2}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{n}(b;q^{2})_{n}}. (1.11)

This family contains, in particular, the shifted denominator (q,q2)n+1(q;q^{2})_{n+1} occurring in (1.2) via the specialization b=q3b=q^{3}, and the two-color family of [4] via b=q2​kb=q^{2k}.

For odd n=2​m+1n=2m+1, define the truncated aa-extension of (1.11) by

𝒯m​(q,a,b):=∑j=0mq2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j​(b,q2)j.\mathcal{T}_{m}(q,a;b):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(b;q^{2})_{j}}. (1.12)

Our third theorem is an exact evaluation at a=q±na=q^{\pm n}.

Theorem 3.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Then

𝒯m​(q,q±n,b)=q2​m​(m+1)​(b​q−n−1,q2)m(b,q2)m.\mathcal{T}_{m}(q,q^{\pm n};b)=q^{2m(m+1)}\frac{(bq^{-n-1};q^{2})_{m}}{(b;q^{2})_{m}}. (1.13)
Corollary 3.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Then modulo (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}), we have

𝒯m​(q,a,b)≡q2​m​(m+1)​(b​q−n−1,q2)m(b,q2)m.\mathcal{T}_{m}(q,a;b)\equiv q^{2m(m+1)}\frac{(bq^{-n-1};q^{2})_{m}}{(b;q^{2})_{m}}. (1.14)
Remark 1.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 and define

cj​(q,a,b):=q2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j​(b,q2)j.c_{j}(q,a;b):=q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(b;q^{2})_{j}}.

Then

∑r=0n−1∑j=0rcj​(q,q±n,b)​cr−j​(q,q±n,b)=q4​m​(m+1)​(b​q−n−1,q2)m2(b,q2)m2.\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^{r}c_{j}(q,q^{\pm n};b)c_{r-j}(q,q^{\pm n};b)=q^{4m(m+1)}\frac{(bq^{-n-1};q^{2})_{m}^{2}}{(b;q^{2})_{m}^{2}}.

This is exactly the same convolution-to-square step used in [8, Lemma 1(a) and equation (14)]. Indeed, cj​(q,q±n,b)=0c_{j}(q,q^{\pm n};b)=0 for j>mj>m, so the left-hand side is

(∑j=0mcj​(q,q±n,b))2,\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{m}c_{j}(q,q^{\pm n};b)\Bigr)^{2},

and Theorem 3 evaluates this square. By the same interpolation argument as in Corollary 3, one also gets

∑r=0n−1∑j=0rcj​(q,a,b)​cr−j​(q,a,b)≡q4​m​(m+1)​(b​q−n−1,q2)m2(b,q2)m2(mod(a−qn)​(1−a​qn)).\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^{r}c_{j}(q,a;b)c_{r-j}(q,a;b)\equiv q^{4m(m+1)}\frac{(bq^{-n-1};q^{2})_{m}^{2}}{(b;q^{2})_{m}^{2}}\pmod{(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n})}.

We next record two useful collections of specializations of Corollary 3; their proofs are postponed until Section 6. The first corresponds directly to the ϕ\phi- and ω\omega-type denominator patterns discussed above.

Corollary 4.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Then modulo (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}), we have

∑j=0mq2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}} ≡q2​m​(m+1),\displaystyle\equiv q^{2m(m+1)}, (1.15)
(1−qn)​∑j=0mq2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j​(q,q2)j+1\displaystyle(1-q^{n})\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(q;q^{2})_{j+1}} ≡(−1)m​qm2+2​m,\displaystyle\equiv(-1)^{m}q^{m^{2}+2m}, (1.16)
∑j=0mq2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j​(−q2,q2)j\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(-q^{2};q^{2})_{j}} ≡qm⁡(m+1).\displaystyle\equiv q^{m(m+1)}. (1.17)

Setting a=1a=1 yields the corresponding congruences modulo Φn​(q)2\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}.

The next pair of specializations will be used for the nontrivial pp-adic versions in Section 2.

Corollary 5.

Let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Then modulo (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}), we have

∑j=0mq2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j​(q,q2)j\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(q;q^{2})_{j}} ≡(−1)m​qm2​1−qn1−q,\displaystyle\equiv(-1)^{m}q^{m^{2}}\frac{1-q^{n}}{1-q}, (1.18)
∑j=0mq2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j​(−q,q2)j\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(-q;q^{2})_{j}} ≡qm2​1+qn1+q.\displaystyle\equiv q^{m^{2}}\frac{1+q^{n}}{1+q}. (1.19)

Setting a=1a=1 yields the corresponding congruences modulo Φn​(q)2\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}.

In particular, Corollary 4 includes the shifted denominator (q,q2)n+1(q;q^{2})_{n+1} via the specialization b=q3b=q^{3}, while the choice b=q2​kb=q^{2k} recovers the two-color family

ℱk​(q)=∑n≥0q2​n​(q,q2)n2(q2,q2)n​(q2​k,q2)n.\mathcal{F}_{k}(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{2n}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{n}^{2}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{n}(q^{2k};q^{2})_{n}}.

The case k=1k=1 matches the prime-case congruence of Guo and Zeng [15, Theorem 1.6], while k≥2k\geq 2 yields a family of zero congruences modulo Φn​(q)2\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}.

Section 2 records the two-color consequences and their pp-adic versions. Sections 3 and 4 prove Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, and Theorem 2 and Corollary 2, respectively. Section 5 proves Theorem 3 and Corollary 3, and Section 6 establishes Corollaries 4 and 5. We conclude in Section 7 with a broader conjectural problem for the remaining two-color families.

2. Two-color consequences and pp-adic versions

We now record the two-color specialization of the denominator family and the resulting pp-adic versions.

Corollary 6 (Recovery of the q2​kq^{2k}-subfamily).

Let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. Define

ℱm,k​(q,a):=∑j=0mq2​j​(a​q,q/a,q2)j(q2,q2)j​(q2​k,q2)j.\mathcal{F}_{m,k}(q,a):=\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(q^{2k};q^{2})_{j}}. (2.1)

Then

ℱm,k​(q,a)≡q2​m​(m+1)​(q2​k−n−1,q2)m(q2​k,q2)m(mod(a−qn)​(1−a​qn)).\mathcal{F}_{m,k}(q,a)\equiv q^{2m(m+1)}\frac{(q^{2k-n-1};q^{2})_{m}}{(q^{2k};q^{2})_{m}}\pmod{(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n})}. (2.2)

If Φn​(q)\Phi_{n}(q) is coprime to (q2​k,q2)m(q^{2k};q^{2})_{m} (for instance, whenever 1≤k≤m+11\leq k\leq m+1), then

∑j=0mq2​j​(q,q2)j2(q2,q2)j​(q2​k,q2)j≡q2​m​(m+1)​(q2​k−n−1,q2)m(q2​k,q2)m(modΦn​(q)2).\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{j}^{2}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(q^{2k};q^{2})_{j}}\equiv q^{2m(m+1)}\frac{(q^{2k-n-1};q^{2})_{m}}{(q^{2k};q^{2})_{m}}\pmod{\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}}. (2.3)
Proof.

This is the specialization b=q2​kb=q^{2k} of Corollary 3, followed by a=1a=1 for the cyclotomic form. ∎

Corollary 7 (pp-adic specialization of the q2​kq^{2k}-subfamily).

Let pp be an odd prime, m=(p−1)/2m=(p-1)/2, and let k≥1k\geq 1 be an integer. Then

∑r=0m(2​rr)216r​(k+r−1r)≡{(−1)m(k=1),0(k≥2​ and ​p≥2​k−1),(modp2).\sum_{r=0}^{m}\frac{\binom{2r}{r}^{2}}{16^{r}\binom{k+r-1}{r}}\equiv\begin{cases}(-1)^{m}&(k=1),\\ 0&(k\geq 2\text{ and }p\geq 2k-1),\end{cases}\pmod{p^{2}}. (2.4)
Proof.

As q→1q\to 1, one has the standard asymptotics

(q,q2)r(q2,q2)r→∏j=1r2​j−12​j=(2​rr)4r,(q2,q2)r(q2​k,q2)r→1(k+r−1r).\frac{(q;q^{2})_{r}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{r}}\to\prod_{j=1}^{r}\frac{2j-1}{2j}=\frac{\binom{2r}{r}}{4^{r}},\qquad\frac{(q^{2};q^{2})_{r}}{(q^{2k};q^{2})_{r}}\to\frac{1}{\binom{k+r-1}{r}}.

Thus the left-hand side of (2.3) tends to the sum on the left-hand side of (2.4). Since Φp​(1)=p\Phi_{p}(1)=p, the modulus Φp​(q)2\Phi_{p}(q)^{2} becomes p2p^{2} in the limit.

For k=1k=1, the right-hand side of (2.3) tends to (−1)m(-1)^{m}, yielding the first case of (2.4). For k≥2k\geq 2 and p≥2​k−1p\geq 2k-1, the factor (q2​k−p−1,q2)m(q^{2k-p-1};q^{2})_{m} contains 1−q01-q^{0} and hence vanishes; the stated zero congruence follows. ∎

Corollary 8.

Let pp be an odd prime. Then

∑r=0(p−1)/2(2​rr)4r≡(−1)(p−1)/2​p(modp2).\sum_{r=0}^{(p-1)/2}\frac{\binom{2r}{r}}{4^{r}}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}p\pmod{p^{2}}. (2.5)
Proof.

Let m=(p−1)/2m=(p-1)/2. Specializing Corollary 5 to a=1a=1 and n=pn=p gives

(a−qn)​(a−q−n).(a-q^{n})(a-q^{-n}).

Since

(a−qn)​(a−q−n)=−q−n​(a−qn)​(1−a​qn),(a-q^{n})(a-q^{-n})=-q^{-n}(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}),

the two moduli differ by a unit in ℚ⁡(q)\mathbb{Q}(q), and the stated congruence follows. ∎

Remark 5 (Harmless q→1q\to 1 limits).

Letting q→1q\to 1 in either Theorem 1 or Theorem 2 yields only the trivial identity 1=11=1. Thus the nontrivial pp-adic shadows in this paper come not from the direct limits of the finite-theta identities, but from Theorem 3, Corollaries 4–5, and the two-color specializations recorded in Section 2.

5. Proof of Theorem 3 and Corollary 3

We now prove Theorem 3 and Corollary 3, which underlie Corollaries 4 and 5.

Proof of Theorem 3.

Set Q=q2Q=q^{2}. Then

𝒯m​(q,qn,b)=∑j=0m(Q−m,Qm+1,Q)j(Q,b,Q)j​Qj=ϕ12​(Q−m,Qm+1b,Q,Q).\mathcal{T}_{m}(q,q^{n};b)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\frac{(Q^{-m},Q^{m+1};Q)_{j}}{(Q,b;Q)_{j}}Q^{j}={}_{2}\phi_{1}\!\left(\begin{matrix}Q^{-m},\,Q^{m+1}\\ b\end{matrix};\,Q,Q\right).

A classical terminating ϕ12{}_{2}\phi_{1} summation (see, for example, [12, eq. (1.5.1)]) gives

ϕ12​(Q−m,AC,Q,Q)=Am​(C/A,Q)m(C,Q)m(m∈ℕ).{}_{2}\phi_{1}\!\left(\begin{matrix}Q^{-m},\,A\\ C\end{matrix};\,Q,Q\right)=A^{m}\frac{(C/A;Q)_{m}}{(C;Q)_{m}}\qquad(m\in\mathbb{N}).

Applying this with A=Qm+1A=Q^{m+1} and C=bC=b yields

𝒯m​(q,qn,b)=Qm⁡(m+1)​(b​Q−m−1,Q)m(b,Q)m=q2​m​(m+1)​(b​q−n−1,q2)m(b,q2)m.\mathcal{T}_{m}(q,q^{n};b)=Q^{m(m+1)}\frac{(bQ^{-m-1};Q)_{m}}{(b;Q)_{m}}=q^{2m(m+1)}\frac{(bq^{-n-1};q^{2})_{m}}{(b;q^{2})_{m}}.

The case a=q−na=q^{-n} is identical, since the summand in (1.12) is invariant under a↦a−1a\mapsto a^{-1}. ∎

Proof of Corollary 3.

By Theorem 3, the difference in (1.14) vanishes at a=qna=q^{n} and a=q−na=q^{-n}. For fixed qq and bb, it is a Laurent polynomial in aa, and multiplying by ama^{m} clears negative powers. Symmetry under a↦a−1a\mapsto a^{-1} then shows divisibility by (a−qn)​(a−q−n)(a-q^{n})(a-q^{-n}). This differs from (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}) only by the unit −q−n-q^{-n}. ∎

Proof of Corollary 4.

The three congruences follow from Corollary 3 by the specializations b=0b=0, q3q^{3}, and −q2-q^{2}, respectively.

For b=0b=0 we use (0,q2)j=1(0;q^{2})_{j}=1 and obtain (1.15). Setting a=1a=1 yields

∑j=0mq2​j​(q,q2)j2(q2,q2)j≡q2​m​(m+1)(modΦn​(q)2).\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{j}^{2}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}}\equiv q^{2m(m+1)}\pmod{\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}}. (6.1)

For b=q3b=q^{3} we use

(q,q2)j+1=(1−q)​(q3,q2)j(q;q^{2})_{j+1}=(1-q)(q^{3};q^{2})_{j}

(q2−n,q2)m(q3,q2)m=(−1)m​q−m2​1−q1−qn.\frac{(q^{2-n};q^{2})_{m}}{(q^{3};q^{2})_{m}}=(-1)^{m}q^{-m^{2}}\frac{1-q}{1-q^{n}}.

and Corollary 3 yields (1.16). Setting a=1a=1 gives

(1−qn)​∑j=0mq2​j​(q,q2)j2(q2,q2)j​(q,q2)j+1≡(−1)m​qm2+2​m(modΦn​(q)2).(1-q^{n})\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{j}^{2}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(q;q^{2})_{j+1}}\equiv(-1)^{m}q^{m^{2}+2m}\pmod{\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}}. (6.3)

For b=−q2b=-q^{2} we use

q2​m​(m+1)​(−q1−n,q2)m(−q2,q2)m=qm⁡(m+1)q^{2m(m+1)}\frac{(-q^{1-n};q^{2})_{m}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{m}}=q^{m(m+1)}

and obtain (1.17). Setting a=1a=1 gives

∑j=0mq2​j​(q,q2)j2(q2,q2)j​(−q2,q2)j≡qm⁡(m+1)(modΦn​(q)2).\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{j}^{2}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}(-q^{2};q^{2})_{j}}\equiv q^{m(m+1)}\pmod{\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}}. (6.4)

∎

Proof of Corollary 5.

These are the specializations b=qb=q and b=−qb=-q of Corollary 3. We use

(q−n,q2)m(q,q2)m=(−1)m​q−m2−2​m​1−qn1−q,(−q−n,q2)m(−q,q2)m=q−m2−2​m​1+qn1+q.\frac{(q^{-n};q^{2})_{m}}{(q;q^{2})_{m}}=(-1)^{m}q^{-m^{2}-2m}\frac{1-q^{n}}{1-q},\qquad\frac{(-q^{-n};q^{2})_{m}}{(-q;q^{2})_{m}}=q^{-m^{2}-2m}\frac{1+q^{n}}{1+q}.

∑j=0mq2​j​(q,q2)j(q2,q2)j\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m}q^{2j}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{j}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{j}} ≡(−1)m​qm2​1−qn1−q(modΦn​(q)2),\displaystyle\equiv(-1)^{m}q^{m^{2}}\frac{1-q^{n}}{1-q}\pmod{\Phi_{n}(q)^{2}}, (6.5)

7. Outlook on the two-color sequences

We conclude by returning to the broader two-color families introduced in [4]:

𝒞k​(q)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{k}(q) :=∑n≥0q2​n​(q,q2)n2(−q2,q2)n​(−q2​k,q2)n,\displaystyle:=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{2n}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{n}^{2}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}(-q^{2k};q^{2})_{n}}, (7.1)
𝒢k​(q)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{k}(q) :=∑n≥0q2​n​(q,q2)n​(−q,q2)n(q2,q2)n​(−q2​k,q2)n,\displaystyle:=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{2n}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{n}(-q;q^{2})_{n}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{n}(-q^{2k};q^{2})_{n}}, (7.2)
ℋk​(q)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{k}(q) :=∑n≥0q2​n​(q,q2)n​(−q,q2)n(q2,q2)n​(q2​k,q2)n.\displaystyle:=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{2n}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{n}(-q;q^{2})_{n}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{n}(q^{2k};q^{2})_{n}}. (7.3)

As k→∞k\to\infty, the family (7.1) tends to

∑n≥0q2​n​(q,q2)n2(−q2,q2)n,\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{2n}\frac{(q;q^{2})_{n}^{2}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}},

which differs from (1.4) only by the initial factor qq. It is therefore natural to ask for microscope congruences for truncated versions of (7.1)–(7.3), ideally with finite theta evaluations at a=q±na=q^{\pm n} analogous to Theorems 1, 2, and 3.

Conjecture 4.

Fix k≥1k\geq 1 and let n=2​m+1n=2m+1 be odd. For each of the series in (7.1)–(7.3), define a natural aa-extension by replacing (q,q2)j2(q;q^{2})_{j}^{2} with (a​q,q/a,q2)j(aq,q/a;q^{2})_{j} and (q,q2)j​(−q,q2)j(q;q^{2})_{j}(-q;q^{2})_{j} with a suitable two-parameter analogue. Then the corresponding truncations at j=mj=m should satisfy microscopic congruences modulo (a−qn)​(1−a​qn)(a-q^{n})(1-aq^{n}) whose specializations at a=q±na=q^{\pm n} are expressible in terms of finite theta polynomials or short linear combinations thereof.

Remark 6.

At present we do not have closed forms analogous to (1.13) for the (−q2,q2)j(-q^{2};q^{2})_{j} denominator families in (7.1) and (7.2). The proved behavior of the ϕ\phi-type and ν\nu-type theorems suggests that such formulas, if they exist, may involve finite theta sums rather than a single qq-Pochhammer quotient. This is the main structural reason for separating the paper into the finite-theta part of Sections 3 and 4 and the exactly summable denominator family based on Theorem 3, Corollaries 4–5, and Section 2. More conceptually, Conjecture 4 should be viewed as part of a broader bridge between mock theta functions and creative microscoping. Ramanujan’s original definition is local at roots of unity, and creative microscoping is local at roots of unity as well. The finite theta polynomials appearing in this paper may therefore be viewed as local theta corrections for truncated mock-theta-type sums. From that viewpoint, it would be more surprising for the remaining two-color families to lie permanently outside the scope of a mock-theta qq-microscope than for them to admit more complicated finite theta descriptions.
